choices.text: The first 25 MB it finds

choices.text: All 28 MB, compressed below the quota

choices.text: Documents/, where the Files app shows them

choices.text: Library/Preferences/

choices.why: Nothing fails; the folder is skipped.

choices.text: It is restored, so the server sees the same device as before

prompt: Which of these belongs in key-value storage such as DataStore, UserDefaults or MMKV?

prompt: A settings file is rewritten in place, and the phone's battery dies halfway through. What does the next launch find, and why does the rename approach avoid it?

choices.text: Half a file; a rename replaces the whole file in one step
choices.why: Right. The reader sees the old file or the new one, never a mixture.

choices.text: The new file, because writes finish when power returns
choices.why: Nothing finishes a write after the power is gone.

choices.text: An empty file, which the app reads as default settings

choices.why: The planner uses a new index at once.

prompt: Inserting a thousand sessions one statement at a time is slow, and wrapping them in one transaction makes it fast. Why?

choices.text: One wait for the disk instead of a thousand
choices.why: Right. The wait for the disk is paid once instead of a thousand times.

choices.text: SQLite skips the checks inside a transaction
choices.why: Constraints are checked either way.

choices.text: The rows go to memory and are lost if the app crashes
choices.why: A committed transaction is as durable as a single statement.

choices.text: A transaction compresses the rows before writing them
choices.why: Nothing is compressed.

prompt: SQLite's write-ahead log is turned on with PRAGMA journal_mode = ___.
Why does the planner make a session's id on the device instead of using AUTOINCREMENT?

choices.text: AUTOINCREMENT is not available in SQLite on phones
choices.why: It exists; it is the wrong tool for rows two devices create.

choices.text: UUIDs are shorter and save space
choices.why: They are longer; the gain is that they are unique without asking anyone.

choices.text: Offline devices would each make the same numbers
choices.why: Right. A random UUID made on the device collides with nobody's.

choices.text: The id must be secret
choices.why: An id is not a secret; it is an address.

prompt: The planner stores each course's minutes for the week on the course row, so the list screen needs no SUM. What must every write of a session do now?

choices.text: Update the course's total in the same transaction
choices.why: Right. Otherwise a crash between the two writes leaves them disagreeing.

choices.text: Send the new total to the server first
choices.why: The server is not involved in keeping a local copy right.

choices.text: Nothing; the list recomputes the totals when it opens
choices.why: Then the stored total is pointless; the list reads it rather than computing it.

choices.text: Lock the course table until the week ends
choices.why: Nothing needs to be locked beyond the transaction.

prompt: Which of these are reasons a phone holds less than the server does? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the device keeps one person's data, not everybody's
choices.why: A device is one account's.

choices.text: old sessions can be fetched on demand rather than kept
choices.why: A window of time keeps it small.

choices.text: SQLite on a phone is limited to one table
choices.why: SQLite on a phone has as many tables as anywhere.

choices.text: the server refuses to send more than a week
choices.why: Nothing refuses; it is a choice the app makes.

prompt: A phone runs version 1 of the planner's schema, and the person installs the update with version 4. What must the migration code do?

choices.text: Delete the database and download it again
choices.why: That loses every change not yet synced.

choices.text: Run step 4, which describes the final shape
choices.why: Step 4 assumes version 3; on a version 1 database it fails or does the wrong thing.

choices.text: Run steps 2, 3 and 4 in order, from user_version 1
choices.why: Right. Each step takes the database from one version to the next.

choices.text: Refuse to open until the person installs versions 2 and 3
choices.why: Nobody can install old versions in order; the app has to take every path.

prompt: A migration step adds a column, then fails while copying data, and it ran inside one transaction. What is on the disk afterwards?

choices.text: The new column and half the copied data
choices.why: That is what happens without the transaction.

choices.text: The database as it was before the step, at the old user_version
choices.why: Right. The rollback undoes the column too, and the next launch can try again.

choices.text: An empty database, because SQLite discards a file whose migration failed
choices.why: Nothing is discarded; the rollback restores what was there.

choices.text: The new column with no data, and user_version raised
choices.why: The version is raised inside the same transaction, so it is undone too.

prompt: Why is Room's fallbackToDestructiveMigration dangerous for an offline-first app in particular?

choices.why: It changes nothing about speed.

choices.text: Google Play rejects apps that use it
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: It runs on the main thread
choices.why: Where it runs is not the danger; what it deletes is.

choices.text: The unsynced changes go with it

Why does the course run every example in Node rather than on Android or iOS?

choices.text: Node is faster than a phone
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Phones cannot run SQLite
choices.why: Both platforms ship it.

choices.text: All three share the problems

choices.text: The stores forbid offline storage
choices.why: They forbid nothing of the kind.

prompt: A Node program saved in ~/notes imports better-sqlite3, which is installed in ~/planner. What happens?

choices.text: A warning about the module type, and then it runs

choices.text: npm downloads it on the fly

prompt: A list of a person's 2,000 sessions is kept in UserDefaults as one array. What does the lesson on key-value storage say goes wrong?

prompt: Which of these change when the planner's data moves from memory into SQLite on the device? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the sessions survive the app being closed
choices.why: That is what being on the disk means.

choices.text: the screen can ask for one week without loading every session
choices.why: A query reads what it asks for.

choices.text: a change to the shape of the data now needs a migration
choices.why: The old shape is on the disk of every phone.

choices.text: the server no longer has to keep the data
choices.why: The device holds a copy of the person's data; the server still keeps it.

prompt: A phone's screen refreshes 120 times a second. How many milliseconds does the app have to produce each frame? Answer to one decimal place.

choices.text: Nothing, because SQLite answers from memory

choices.text: The list freezes for about eighteen frames at 60 Hz
choices.why: Right. Nothing is drawn while the thread waits on the query.

choices.text: An Application Not Responding dialog at once

choices.text: The query is moved to another thread by the system
choices.why: The system moves nothing; the app chooses where it runs.

prompt: better-sqlite3 is synchronous. In Node, a timer is due during a long query. When does it fire?

choices.text: Never; the timer is cancelled
choices.why: It is delayed, not cancelled.

choices.text: Halfway through, pausing the query

prompt: In an offline-first planner, where does the week screen read its sessions from?

choices.text: From the server, falling back to the database when offline

choices.text: From memory, filled at start-up from the server

choices.why: Right. The write is real now; the mark tells the truth about sync.

choices.text: The session, with no mark, as if it were synced

choices.text: Retry it until the server accepts

choices.why: A change that disappears without a word is the worst outcome.

choices.text: Delete the session from the device
choices.why: That destroys what the person typed.

choices.text: SQLite allows one write per transaction
choices.why: A transaction holds as many writes as it needs.

choices.text: A crash could separate them

choices.text: The server reads the transaction log
choices.why: The server never sees the device's database.

choices.text: A delete of s9
choices.why: The server never heard of s9, so there is nothing to delete.

choices.text: The three, in order

prompt: One operation in the outbox is refused with 400 every time. The drain stops at the first failure. What happens, and what does the lesson do about it?

choices.text: It clears itself after an hour
choices.why: A 400 does not change with time.

choices.text: The server accepts it on the fifth try
choices.why: A refusal for the content is the same on every try.

choices.text: The drain skips it and the order of later operations does not matter
choices.why: Order matters when operations depend on each other, which is why skipping is a decision.

choices.text: The queue waits behind it until it is set aside
choices.why: Right. A poison operation blocks the queue until it is taken out of it.

prompt: Which of these answers should the planner retry? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a connection that timed out
choices.why: The network failed, which says nothing about the server.

choices.text: 503 Service Unavailable
choices.why: The server says it cannot answer now.

choices.text: 429 Too Many Requests
choices.why: Later, and as slowly as the server asks.

choices.text: 400 Bad Request
choices.why: The request is wrong; sending it again sends the same mistake.

choices.text: 403 Forbidden
choices.why: Being refused permission does not change by repeating.

prompt: Why does the planner add random jitter to its exponential backoff?

choices.why: Full jitter makes the average wait shorter, but that is not why it exists.

choices.text: Because servers refuse requests at exact intervals
choices.why: No server does that.

choices.text: So the phones that failed together do not all retry together
choices.why: Right. Without it, an outage ends with every phone arriving in the same second.

choices.text: To hide the app's traffic from the network
choices.why: It hides nothing.

prompt: A backoff starts at 1 second and doubles each attempt, capped at 60 seconds. What is the ceiling of the wait before the eighth attempt (after seven failures), in seconds?

choices.text: In two minutes
choices.why: Right. The server knows its load; the client does not.

choices.text: In 124 seconds, the two added
choices.why: Retry-After is the wait, not an extra on top of one.

choices.text: In 4 seconds; the client's schedule decides
choices.why: The server has said when it can take more; ignoring it earns another 429.

choices.text: Not at all
choices.why: 429 is temporary by definition.

prompt: The planner sends POST /sessions, the server saves the session, and the response is lost on the way back. The planner retries. Without an idempotency key, what does the server hold?

choices.text: One session and an error
choices.why: Nothing refused the second.

choices.text: One session, since the server notices the repeat
choices.why: Nothing lets it notice; that is what the key is for.

choices.text: None, because the first request was lost
choices.why: The request arrived; the response was lost.

choices.text: Two sessions
choices.why: Right. From the server's side the retry is a new request.

prompt: Where does the planner make an operation's idempotency key, and when?

choices.text: On the server, when the request arrives
choices.why: The server cannot tell a retry from a new request without a key the client sent.

choices.text: On the device, once per operation
choices.why: Right. Every attempt of that operation carries the same key.

choices.text: On the device, fresh for every attempt
choices.why: A new key per attempt makes every retry look new.

choices.text: From the session's date and minutes
choices.why: Two real sessions can share a date and a length.

prompt: A request arrives with a key the server has stored, but its body is different from the first. What should the server do?

choices.text: Return the stored response, as for any repeat
choices.why: The stored response answers a different request; returning it hides a client bug.

choices.text: Refuse it
choices.why: Right. A key names one operation; a different body is a misuse.

choices.text: Apply the new body and overwrite the stored response
choices.why: Then the key no longer protects anything.

choices.text: Apply both and return both
choices.why: That is the duplicate the key exists to prevent.

prompt: Why is PUT /sessions/{id}, with an id the device made, idempotent where POST /sessions is not?

choices.text: PUT requests are never retried by clients
choices.why: They are retried; repeating one is harmless.

choices.text: PUT is encrypted and POST is not
choices.why: Both travel the same way.

choices.text: Servers store PUT responses for 24 hours
choices.why: That is what an idempotency key asks of a server; PUT needs nothing stored.

choices.text: It states the result, not an action
choices.why: Right. The second PUT leaves the same row; the second POST makes a new one.

prompt: The header a client sends so the server can recognise a retried request is called ___.

choices.text: 409 Conflict, to be retried later
choices.why: Right. The second must neither run nor pretend to have an answer.

choices.text: The stored response, which does not exist yet
choices.why: There is nothing stored to return while the first is still running.

choices.text: It runs both, since neither has a stored response
choices.why: That is the double charge the key was meant to stop.

choices.text: 200 with an empty body
choices.why: A success that did nothing would lie to the client.

choices.text: The cursor encrypts the request
choices.why: It encrypts nothing.

choices.text: Nothing; the server converts the time zone

choices.text: The server refuses the request
choices.why: It accepts any time it is given.

choices.text: The person's choice of light or dark theme
choices.why: Right. The latest choice is the one they want, and losing the older one costs nothing.

choices.text: A shared list of courses that two people add to
choices.why: One person's additions would replace the other's.

choices.text: A note two people edit at once
choices.why: One person's text would vanish.

prompt: The planner sends PUT with version 3, the version it read, and the server's row is at version 4. What does the server answer?

choices.text: 200, and the row becomes version 5
choices.why: That would overwrite a change the phone never saw.

choices.text: 412 with the row deleted
choices.why: Nothing is deleted.

choices.text: 404, because version 3 no longer exists
choices.why: The row exists; the version is out of date.

choices.text: 409 Conflict, because somebody changed the row since it was read
choices.why: Right. The client must read version 4 and decide again.

prompt: Vector clocks {phone: 2, tablet: 1} and {phone: 1, tablet: 2}. What does comparing them say?

choices.text: They are concurrent: each has seen something the other has not
choices.why: Right. Neither is greater in every entry, so neither happened after the other.

choices.text: They are equal, since both sum to 3
choices.why: Sums are not compared; each entry is.

choices.text: The first is newer, because it is listed first
choices.why: Order in the list means nothing.

choices.text: The second is newer, because the tablet synced last
choices.why: When it synced is not in the clock; what each device had seen is.

prompt: Base: 30 minutes, not done. The phone sets minutes to 45. The tablet marks it done. A field-by-field three-way merge gives what?

choices.text: 45 minutes, not done; the phone wrote last
choices.why: That is last write wins on the whole row.

choices.text: 30 minutes, done; the base wins where they disagree
choices.why: The base is what both started from, not a winner.

choices.text: 45 minutes, done
choices.why: Right. Each side changed a different field, so both changes survive.

choices.text: A conflict for the person to settle
choices.why: There is no conflict: no field was changed on both sides.

prompt: A merge that compares both versions with the version they started from is called a ___-way merge.
When does the lesson say the planner should ask the person to settle a conflict?

choices.text: When one field changed on both sides
choices.why: Right. That is the case where any automatic choice throws away somebody's intent.

choices.text: Never; the server decides
choices.why: Some conflicts have no rule that is right, and the person knows which edit they meant.

choices.text: On every sync, so they stay in control
choices.why: Asking about what the merge can settle trains people to tap without reading.

choices.text: When the person has been offline for more than a day
choices.why: Time offline is not what makes a conflict.

prompt: Match each merge property of a CRDT to what it means.

pairs.right: merging A into B gives what merging B into A gives
the grouping of three merges does not matter
merging the same state twice changes nothing

right_distractors: the newest write replaces the others

prompt: A G-counter of sessions done holds {phone: 3, tablet: 2}. The phone merges in {phone: 1, tablet: 4}. What is the merged state, and its value?

choices.text: {phone: 4, tablet: 6}, value 10
choices.why: Adding the entries counts the same increments twice.

choices.text: {phone: 1, tablet: 4}, value 5
choices.why: That replaces the local state with the incoming one.

choices.text: {phone: 3, tablet: 4}, value 7
choices.why: Right. Merge takes the maximum of each entry; the value is their sum.

choices.text: {phone: 3, tablet: 2}, value 5
choices.why: That ignores what the tablet counted.

prompt: A G-counter merges {phone: 5, tablet: 1, laptop: 2} with {phone: 2, tablet: 3, laptop: 2}. What is the counter's value after the merge?
In an OR-set, the phone removes the course Guitar while the tablet, offline, adds Guitar again. After both merge, is Guitar in the set?

choices.text: No, removes always beat adds
choices.why: That would be a different set, and it would lose the tablet's add.

choices.text: Yes, the add it never saw survives
choices.why: Right. The tablet's new add has a tag the phone never removed.

choices.text: It depends on which device merged first
choices.why: A CRDT gives the same result in any order.

choices.text: It appears twice
choices.why: A set holds an element once.

prompt: What does a CRDT library such as Yjs or Automerge cost an app, which a plain table of sessions does not?

choices.text: A server that runs the merge
choices.why: Merges run on each device; that is the point.

choices.text: Licences per device
choices.why: Both are open-source libraries.

choices.text: It stops the app from querying the data with SQL
choices.why: It changes how the data is kept, but the app can still index what it needs elsewhere.

choices.text: Metadata that keeps growing
choices.why: Right. Merging without coordination needs to remember what each side did.

prompt: Two Yjs documents edit the same map offline. How do they converge?

choices.text: The server picks one document and sends it to both
choices.why: No document is picked; both edits are merged.

choices.text: The person merges them by hand
choices.why: The library merges them.

choices.text: Each applies the other's update
choices.why: Right. encodeStateAsUpdate on one side, applyUpdate on the other, in either order.

choices.text: They do not; Yjs needs both to be online
choices.why: Offline edits are exactly what it handles.

prompt: What is the shortest repeat interval WorkManager allows for a periodic job, in minutes?
An iOS planner submits a BGAppRefreshTask request for every hour. What does it get?

choices.text: Runs when the system decides
choices.why: Right. iOS weighs battery, network and how the person uses the app.

choices.text: A run every hour, on the hour
choices.why: The earliest begin date is a floor, not a schedule.

choices.text: A refusal, because refresh tasks are for apps with an active audio session
choices.why: Audio is a separate background mode.

choices.text: Unlimited time while the phone is charging
choices.why: That is closer to a processing task, and still not unlimited.

prompt: A person force-quits the planner from the iOS app switcher. What happens to its scheduled background refresh?

choices.text: It runs as scheduled; force-quitting only closes the screen
choices.why: iOS reads a force-quit as the person not wanting the app to run.

choices.text: It runs once to save the data, then stops
choices.why: There is no final run.

choices.text: It moves to a background URLSession
choices.why: Nothing moves on its own.

choices.text: It does not run until the person opens the app again
choices.why: Right. That is why the sync must also run when the app comes to the foreground.

prompt: Why does the lesson's sync take a budget and save its cursor as it goes?

choices.text: To make each sync faster
choices.why: The work is the same; it is split so it survives.

choices.text: So an interrupted run picks up where it stopped
choices.why: Right. Work finished before the stop is kept.

choices.text: Because the server allows one request a minute
choices.why: The budget is about the device's limits.

choices.text: To save battery by syncing less data
choices.why: All the data still syncs, over more runs.

prompt: Match each mechanism to its platform.

pairs.right: Android
iOS
React Native with Expo

prompt: The planner asks for a course's details with If-None-Match and the ETag it has. The server answers 304. What does the planner do?

choices.text: Deletes its copy, which the server says is wrong
choices.why: 304 says the copy is still right.

choices.text: Keeps its copy and marks it fresh again
choices.why: Right. Nothing was sent but the answer; the body it has is current.

choices.text: Downloads it again without the header
choices.why: That wastes the request 304 just saved.

choices.text: Shows an error: 304 is a redirect
choices.why: It is in the 3xx range, but it means not modified.

prompt: Stale-while-revalidate: the cached week is two hours past its expiry and the person opens it offline. What do they see?

choices.text: An empty screen until the network returns
choices.why: That throws away a copy that is better than nothing.

choices.text: An error saying the data expired
choices.why: Expired means ask again, not refuse to show.

choices.text: The copy, with no sign of its age
choices.why: Showing it is right; hiding that it is old is not.

choices.text: The stale copy, marked as old
choices.why: Right. Show what is there, and refresh behind it.

prompt: An LRU cache bounded at 50 MB receives a 4 MB picture while holding 48 MB. Put its steps in order.
items: see that 48 + 4 is over 50
evict the least recently used entries until it fits
store the new picture
record it as the most recently used

prompt: Why must the planner never keep the only copy of anything in Library/Caches/ or cache/?

choices.text: The system clears them under pressure, without asking
choices.why: Right. Whatever is there must be fetchable again.

choices.text: Files there are encrypted with a key the app cannot read
choices.why: The app reads them like any of its own.

choices.text: Those folders are readable by other apps
choices.why: They are inside the sandbox like the rest.

choices.text: They are not counted in the app's storage
choices.why: They are counted; the person sees them in the app's size.

prompt: Why does the planner store an attachment as a file with its path in a row, rather than as a BLOB in SQLite?

choices.text: Files are encrypted and rows are not
choices.why: Encryption is a separate decision, lesson 19's.

choices.text: SQLite cannot store binary data
choices.why: It can; the question is whether it should.

choices.text: Blobs bloat the database
choices.why: Right. The row keeps what the query needs; the bytes stay on the disk.

choices.text: The server can read files but not rows
choices.why: The server reads neither; it receives what the app sends.

prompt: A download stopped at 3 MB of 8. What does the planner send to resume it, and what does a server that supports it answer?

choices.text: Range: bytes=3145728-; 206 Partial Content with the rest
choices.why: Right. The offset is the size of the part on the disk.

choices.text: The same request again; 200 with the whole file
choices.why: That starts over and throws away 3 MB.

choices.text: If-None-Match with the ETag; 304
choices.why: That asks whether the whole thing changed, not for a part of it.

choices.text: Content-Length: 5 MB; 201
choices.why: That header describes a body the client sends.

prompt: A download into the planner's files fails with ENOSPC halfway. What must the code make sure of before it reports the failure?

choices.text: That the row says the attachment is there, so the next launch can find the part
choices.why: A row that claims a whole file over half a file is the defect.

choices.text: That it retries at once, since space comes back by itself
choices.why: A full disk is not a network blip; retrying at once fails the same way.

choices.text: That no row points at the half-written file as if it were whole
choices.why: Right. Write to a temporary name, and record the row only once the file is complete.

choices.text: That the database is deleted to free space
choices.why: That destroys the person's data to make room for a download.

prompt: Which of these does a sweep for orphans find? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a file in attachments/ that no row names
choices.why: It costs disk and nothing uses it.

choices.text: a row naming a file that is not on the disk
choices.why: The screen would show an attachment that cannot open.

choices.text: a session with no attachment
choices.why: That is ordinary; most sessions have none.

choices.text: a file in the cache that was used yesterday
choices.why: That is the cache working.

prompt: Which of these does encrypting the planner's data at rest protect against?

choices.text: Malware running inside the app while it is open
choices.why: Code running as the app reads what the app reads.

choices.text: A lost phone, read while locked
choices.why: Right. Without the key, what is on the disk is noise.

choices.text: A server that leaks the person's data
choices.why: The server is a different copy, with its own protection.

choices.text: The person forgetting their password
choices.why: Encryption makes that worse, not better.

prompt: The planner encrypts two notes with AES-256-GCM, the same key and the same nonce. What has gone wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; a nonce is only checked when decrypting
choices.why: Reuse breaks the encryption itself, not a check.

choices.text: Decryption fails for the second note
choices.why: Both decrypt; that is why the mistake goes unnoticed.

choices.text: The notes become twice as large
choices.why: Size does not change.

choices.text: It leaks and allows forgeries
choices.why: Right. Each encryption under a key needs a fresh nonce.

prompt: A byte of an encrypted note is changed on the disk. What happens when the planner decrypts it with AES-GCM?

choices.text: The note comes back with one wrong letter
choices.why: GCM does not hand back altered text.

choices.text: It decrypts, and a warning is logged
choices.why: There is no partial success.

choices.text: Decryption fails
choices.why: Right. Tampering is detected rather than decrypted.

choices.text: The key is rotated
choices.why: Nothing rotates on its own.

prompt: Why does the lesson wrap the data key with a key kept in the Keystore or Keychain, rather than store the data key beside the data?

choices.text: A copy would carry its own key
choices.why: Right. The disk holds the data key only in wrapped form.

choices.text: A wrapped key encrypts faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The Keystore requires it
choices.why: It requires nothing; it is the safer arrangement.

choices.text: So the server can decrypt the data
choices.why: The server never sees either key.

prompt: What should a biometric unlock of the planner's notes actually do?

choices.text: Set a flag in preferences that the notes may be shown
choices.why: A flag can be flipped without the finger; the notes are still readable.

choices.text: Send the fingerprint to the server to be checked
choices.why: The biometric never leaves the device.

choices.text: Store the fingerprint image in the keychain
choices.why: The app never receives the fingerprint.

choices.text: Release a key from the secure hardware that decrypts the notes
choices.why: Right. Without the biometric there is no key, so there is nothing to bypass.

prompt: On iOS, a file protected with the class NSFileProtection___ cannot be read while the device is locked.
The planner's JavaScript bundle contains an API key for a paid service. Who can read it?

choices.text: Nobody, since the bundle is minified
choices.why: Minifying renames variables; the key stays a plain string.

choices.text: Anybody who installs the app
choices.why: Right. A secret shipped to every device is not a secret; a server should hold it.

choices.text: Only someone who breaks the store's encryption
choices.why: The installed app is on the person's device, readable to them.

choices.text: Google and Apple, nobody else
choices.why: The file is on every phone that installed it.

prompt: Where does the planner keep its refresh token, and what does signing out do to it?

choices.text: In preferences, and signing out leaves it for the next sign-in
choices.why: Preferences are plain files, and a token left behind signs the next person in.

choices.text: In the keystore, wiped at sign-out
choices.why: Right. Signing out must leave nothing that signs anybody in.

choices.text: In the database beside the sessions, kept after sign-out
choices.why: A token in the database goes into its backups and stays.

choices.text: Nowhere; the password is stored instead
choices.why: Storing the password is worse in every way.

prompt: A crash log uploaded by the planner contains the person's e-mail address. Which principle of the last lesson did it break?

choices.text: Encryption at rest, because logs are not encrypted
choices.why: Encrypting the log would still send the address away.

choices.text: Backup rules, because logs go into the backup
choices.why: Where the log is kept is secondary to what it carries.

choices.text: Idempotency, because the log may be uploaded twice
choices.why: Duplicates are not the problem; the content is.

choices.text: Keep less: a log has no need of who the person is
choices.why: Right. Data that is not collected cannot leak.

prompt: Match each store requirement to what it is.

pairs.right: Google Play's form about what an app collects and shares
the labels on an App Store page about the data an app uses
Apple's privacy manifest, with the reasons for certain APIs

right_distractors: a file the server sends at sign-in

prompt: A React Native planner opens its database with expo-sqlite. On Android, where does the file end up?

choices.text: Inside the app's private storage, where the platform keeps its databases
choices.why: Right. The library asks the platform; the file is in the sandbox like a Kotlin app's.

choices.text: In a JavaScript heap kept in memory
choices.why: A database in memory would be gone at the next launch.

choices.text: On the SD card
choices.why: Shared storage is not where a private database goes.

choices.text: In Expo's servers
choices.why: The database is on the device.

prompt: The week screen loads page 1 of 20 sessions, a new session is inserted at the top, and page 2 is loaded with OFFSET 20. What does the person see?

choices.text: Page 2 as it would have been
choices.why: Every row moved down by one, so the offset now points one row earlier in the old order.

choices.text: An error, since the table changed
choices.why: Nothing errors; the result is quietly wrong.

choices.text: A row it already showed, repeated
choices.why: Right. Every row moved down one place, so the last of page 1 comes back; keyset paging, which continues after the last row seen, does not repeat it.

choices.text: The new session twice
choices.why: The new session is on page 1.

prompt: The planner drains its outbox in the order the operations were made. Why not send them all at once, in parallel?

choices.text: An update could arrive before the create it depends on
choices.why: Right. Order is part of what the outbox records.

choices.text: It would use more battery
choices.why: That may be true and is not the reason.

choices.text: Servers accept one connection per device
choices.why: They accept many; the order is the issue.

choices.text: SQLite cannot read the outbox twice
choices.why: It can read it as often as it likes.

prompt: For which of these is a CRDT the wrong tool, according to the lesson on CRDT libraries?

choices.text: A shared note two people edit offline
choices.why: That is the case CRDTs were made for.

choices.text: A counter incremented on several devices
choices.why: A G-counter handles exactly that.

choices.text: A booking that must not be given to two people, where somebody has to say no
choices.why: Right. A CRDT accepts every concurrent change; a rule that refuses one needs a single authority.

choices.text: A set of course tags added on two devices
choices.why: An OR-set handles it.

prompt: Which of the three kinds of local data is a course the person has chosen to keep for a flight?

choices.text: Cache, which the system may clear
choices.why: Then it could be gone at the moment the person needs it.

choices.text: Pinned: kept until the person unpins it, out of the reach of eviction
choices.why: Right. The person asked for it, so no size limit may evict it.

choices.text: The source of truth
choices.why: The server holds the course; the device holds a copy on request.

choices.text: Temporary files
choices.why: tmp/ is cleared when the app is not running.

prompt: Before downloading a 200 MB course pack, the planner checks free space. Why, if the write would fail anyway with ENOSPC?

choices.text: ENOSPC is not reported on phones
choices.why: It is; the check is about what happens before it.

choices.text: To make the download faster
choices.why: It changes nothing about speed.

choices.text: The store requires it
choices.why: No store does.

choices.text: To refuse before spending the data plan and filling the disk
choices.why: Right. Failing at 199 MB costs the download and leaves a full disk behind.

prompt: A different person signs in on a phone where the planner holds the previous person's sessions. What must happen before the new person sees a screen?

choices.text: Nothing; the server filters by account
choices.why: The local copy is not filtered by the server; it is on the disk.

choices.text: The old sessions are hidden behind a flag
choices.why: Hidden is still on the device, and still readable.

choices.text: The previous person's data and tokens are wiped, and the new account syncs from scratch
choices.why: Right. Lessons 12 and 20 both end here: a full resync, after a wipe.

choices.text: The new person is asked which sessions to keep
choices.why: They are somebody else's sessions.

prompt: What does Apple's privacy manifest ask an app to declare about certain APIs, such as the one that reads the free disk space?

choices.text: The approved reason the app uses them
choices.why: Right. Each required-reason API is listed with one of Apple's reason codes.

choices.text: How many times a day the app calls them
choices.why: Frequency is not asked for.

choices.text: The server that receives the result
choices.why: That belongs to the data the app collects, not to these APIs.

choices.text: Nothing; it lists only the app's name
choices.why: It lists the reasons, which is the point.
